body.heading: A long time not knowing
paragraphs: Until surprisingly recently, nobody knew whether other stars had planets at all. Planets are small and dark, and their stars are dazzlingly bright, so a planet is like a firefly hovering beside a lighthouse.

The first confirmed planets beyond our solar system were found in 1992, orbiting the spinning remnant of a dead star. In 1995, astronomers found a planet around a sun-like star, 51 Pegasi — a giant world hugging its star far closer than Mercury hugs our Sun, which nobody had expected.

body.heading: How to find an invisible world
paragraphs: Most exoplanets are found indirectly. In the transit method, a telescope watches a star's light dip slightly and regularly, the signature of a planet crossing in front of it. The Kepler space telescope used this trick to find thousands of worlds at once.

Astronomers also watch stars wobble. A planet's gravity tugs its star in a tiny circle, and that wobble, measured in starlight, can reveal the planet's mass even when the planet itself cannot be seen.

body.heading: Worlds stranger than fiction
paragraphs: The catalogue now holds more than 5,500 confirmed planets: lava worlds, puffy giants, planets with two suns, and a few rocky worlds in the temperate zones where liquid water might exist.
None of this proves that life exists elsewhere. But every new world sharpens the question, and the telescopes keep getting better at asking it.

takeaway: We find distant planets not by seeing them, but by watching their stars dim and wobble — and there are thousands of them.
